findings.comment: files_jsonl is JSONL (one object per line, per the comment directly above), but jq without -s applies the filter to each line as a separate input. So any(.[]; .patch != null) is evaluated against a single file object, where .[] yields the object's *values* (strings like the filename and the patch text), not the list of files. Applying .patch to a string raises 'Cannot index string with "patch"', jq exits non-zero (5), and the leading ! classifies that as 'no textual changes' -> exit 0. Net effect: every PR is skipped, including PRs with textual changes — the review pipeline silently no-ops, the opposite of the PR's stated goal. The filter only answers 'does any file have a patch?' if the lines are aggregated into one array first (jq -s).

The '(docs/binary-only?)' hint is misleading: docs-only PRs (markdown edits) produce patches and will not reach this branch. The realistic causes of an all-null patch set are binary-only, mode-only (e.g. chmod), or rename-only changes, so this message can send someone debugging skipped PRs in the wrong direction.
